“And then back downhill, stroller on the curb—”

Zenon flicked a muffin crumb off the notebook cover. “Always assume someone parked in the ramp. People are gifts that way.”

Digits scrolled upward on Prisha’s phone timer, merciless. “So final plan: diapers if I skip the library slot and cut the Hill altogether—less incline, more repeats?”

“If you’re that picky about hills, sure. DoorDash exists for a reason.”

“I know, but I need the steps for sanity. Just don’t make me use that side-street shortcut by the brewery. Do NOT take the brewery alley, the paving’s broken and the dumpster trucks line up at two.”

The mention of trucks seemed to trigger a neuron that didn’t house directions.
speaker: Zenon

story:
Walid stepped between the benches, bamboo held like a fragile summons. “Excuse me — could you spare two minutes? This flute mouthpiece keeps fetching air instead of sound, and I’m down to my last culm.”

Freya glanced at the wall clock. Its second-hand had the reluctant twitch of something overworked and unreplaced. “Sure thing. Make it quick, though — maintenance wants photos, HR wants forms, and noon’s already grumbling at me.”

He laid the culm down and pointed to a faint pencil oval. “I marked an oval where I think the embouchure should go — measured 10 mm from the node, angled thirty degrees — but when I drill even the tiniest pilot, the walls chip out.”

Her gaze slid to the rotary tool, then away. “Different bit, slower feed. Or switch tools; that scarred one’s got plenty of gossip. Grab the micro-files instead, advanced station on the left.”

Walid’s fingers crept protectively around the bamboo. “Whatever you do, do NOT use the rotary tool on this. I ruined two pieces with a 3 mm burr two nights ago; it cost me thirty bucks of bamboo and a week of data. Hand tools only from here.”

Freya nodded with the rhythm of someone tamping down a yawn.
speaker: Freya

story:
The wall-clock clacked to three-thirty as Bryn ducked through the door, messenger bag scraping the threshold. Plaster dust sat on everything like unwashed snow. Twenty-two egg-smooth masks stared at nothing from their dowel fence above the cracked palette.

Celia looked up from the monitor, earbuds swinging like a cut noose. One thumb still moved over the vinegar-smelling wipe, leaving aqua streaks on her knuckle—small, bright signals that she’d rather be anywhere else.

Bryn stopped in front of her. “Hey, could you walk me through using shading alone to make neutral masks read as different faces?”

“I’d love to, but honestly the lighting designer chooses what the audience sees—best to ask them.” The answer came easy, rehearsed, like a flu shot in an express lane.

“The LUT director wants the shade work on the plaster, not the lights. Any starting pigment mix?” Bryn kept the politeness clipped to a cutting edge.

Celia flicked her gaze at the ceiling. “There’s a guy upstairs, Marco, he handles balance plays—has better charts than I do.” Her free hand toyed with the earbud jack, coiling it as if rope might appear.

“I really need it this afternoon and I’ve double-booked your time. Whatever you do, don’t use Flake White—went toxic on me last semester.” Bryn’s tone didn’t ask to be spared.
speaker: Celia

story:
The vats hiss, a slow steam trying to be cicadas in March. Mariam shifts the lab notebook to her hip; violet smears have colonized the cuff of her sweater. She spots Teague polishing the brass tap with the weary precision of someone who wants it to take forever so the bus has nowhere to go.

“Hey, quick question on the filter media grades. We're seeing cloudiness after the 2-micron cellulose pad and I'm wondering if perlite would clear it without stripping too much flavor.”

Teague doesn’t look up. The paper towel squeaks, brass shines, and the clock stares at itself. “Um. Haven’t messed with the fine grades lately—you should ask Troy. He’s on break, back in fifteen.”

“Troy's swamped,” Mariam says. “You're running this half of the line daily; your experience beats another hand-off and a delay. What's the perlite grit that runs clear without over-filter?”

He draws the towel along the tap’s throat one more time because justice. “Bold of you to assume I note the grit. I just swap cartridges when the pressure creeps. Talk to supply crib, end of hallway.” Teague is already picturing the bus turn the corner, diesel sighing with relief.

“Look, if it takes your whole shift to find it you can log the data under my project number. Two minutes with you beats forty with paperwork. So, perlite: E series or F series?”

The paper towel goes into the trash can without a sound. “You’re reading more into my night job than’s there. Check the binder above the scale—pages three through fifteen are probably more literate than I am.”

She snorts. “Binder’s outdated; numbers changed in November.” She points at the cracked sample cup like it’s responsible. “I need current practice. Is F2 finer or coarser than the E1 you ran last month?”

“Honestly? I just match the color code on the box. Green good, yellow not-so-good. That’s the full depth of my insight tonight.” Teague slides his hand into the jacket sleeve, zipper teeth auditioning for escape.

“Then give me the box label, no philosophy. F2 or E1?”

He raises both palms, surrender without guns. “Sure—but whatever you land on, just don’t switch to diatomaceous earth. Last time it plugged the pump so hard we had to tear the manifold apart. DO NOT use diatomaceous earth.” And before she can pounce:
speaker: Teague

story:
Yael pushed past the bins of pompoms that smelled perpetually of kindergarten peanut butter. The social-worker’s note fluttered in her hand like a parking ticket; she had forty minutes between seminar and mid-term. “Do you have a minute?” she asked, steady. “I need to put together a memory box and the caseworker told me you’re the person who knows how they survive being tossed in suitcases.”

Urmi flinched at the sound of footsteps, then went back to snapping floss by hue. The earbuds around their neck sighed with latent music no one would hear. “They don’t really survive, but okay. What size kid?”

“Tall nine-year-old, rough on stuff. I’ve got this USPS flat rate box, but the corners collapse. What do I reinforce with so it lasts past tomorrow?”

“Cardboard corners inside, hot glue. Tape the seams, not the outside art—you’ll mush it. Anything else?” The words came on conveyer belt cadence while Urmi stared at the wall clock and its steady march toward the next fire drill.

“Hinges. I can’t get the lid to open twice without ripping the grain. Duct tape looks terrible.”

“Reinforced paper tape, fabric side out. L-brackets if you have time. There’s a box in the closet.” Urmi’s hand drifted toward the closet but never left the floss, like it had changed its mind halfway across the room.

“We’re painting on top. Acrylic, right? I read the finish cracks if the kid flexes the lid.”

“Acrylic, then matte medium on top. Better yet, skip paint, give him fabric and markers. Less cracking, but it’s your funeral.”

Yael uncapped her pen to write “fabric & markers,” paused, clicked it again. “Last thing—inside lining. Ribbon tears, paper gets wet. I need something cheap and washable. And look, please don’t say felt; felt pills and stains if it meets grape juice.”

Urmi’s gaze crawled up to the ceiling as though instructions were written on the plastic diffuser.
speaker: Urmi

story:
The bell at Greater Metropolitan Notary forgot how to ring long ago, so the only sound that announced Violeta was the soft scuff of sneakers on industrial linoleum. She set her folder on Station 12’s counter; the manila edges kissed the worn plastic that read “Farid.” Sweat had already begun to salt her collar from the walk across the lot.

Farid rotated the cracked name tag until the lighter half faced the wall. “Hi—sorry, do you handle private used-car sales here? I need the bill of sale notarized,” she said.

He flicked a glance at his watch, the leather dark with yesterday’s humidity. “Not me personally—go to Station 3, end of the hall. They have the right seal.”

“I did; they pointed me back here for the paperwork packet itself. Can I get one?”

A fluorescent tube hummed overhead like a captive mosquito. “You’ll need a DR-11 form from the tax office. We just verify signatures, we don’t keep blank packets.”

Her sigh drew a momentary breeze across both of them. “The buyer’s on a deadline; do NOT tell me to drive across town for another form. It’s ninety-five degrees and my AC’s broken. Just give me the list of what I need.”

Farid eased back an inch; the chair gasped.
speaker: Farid

story:
Briony’s coat was already on, scalpel glinting in her pocket like a secret. She’d only ducked back for it—ten seconds, tops—but Ansel was planted between the stuffed curlews and the exit like a man staking claim. He held a padded outstretched box the size of a paperback. Inside, an unlucky Swallowtail posed in compound fracture, one wing pleated the wrong way forever.

“I’ve got a Swallowtail that set its wings at the wrong angle,” he said, voice pitched tight with nerves and Friday exhaustion. “How do I reposition it after pins are already in?”

Briony gave him the three-shoulder version of a shrug—left, right, away. “You can’t. Once scaled and dried, bending risks a stress fracture. Try making the next one fresh.” She started sidestepping toward daylight glimmering off the hallway tile.

“I don’t have a fresh one,” Ansel replied, shifting his weight to block the sidestep. “I need this one for tomorrow’s outreach display. There has to be a trick.”

“Not really. Technique is aim-it-right-when-it-dies. Anything else costs you iridescence.” The automatic fan behind them finished a slow revolution with its metal tick.

He checked the skylight without meaning to—sun sliding west fast. “What about controlled humidity? A dome with wet sponge, slow rehydrate, then quick rebend?”

“Whole wing will bloom mildew before it flexes. Trust me, ten-minute pitch with kids beats no wings.”

Ansel rolled tongue against teeth, tasting something resinous. “There’s no alternative? I was told you mounted a Ghost Mantis that started stiff twice.”

“That was acrylic coat and week-long clamp. Takes longer than your deadline allows. Ciao.” Briony flicked the keys at her hip—clack, clack—stepping right. He stepped with her.

“Wait—one last thought,” he said, dogged. “Going back to the library’s freeze-dry rig and snap-vac reheating?”
speaker: Briony

story:
The ceiling bulb flickers once, as if shrugging: forty watts can’t solve everything. Enrique scoots forward on the injection-molded stool; his laptop bag scratches the plexiglass like plastic on teeth.

“Neto’s out in thirty-nine days. What’s the fastest legal way to get him a photo ID before he hits the gate?”

Paloma keeps her eyes on the yellowed wall clock fashioned into a sheriff badge. “You’d need to ask the discharge planner downstairs. I just monitor visits.”

He unzips the bag, producing a wrinkled checklist printed on low-budget copy paper. “I tried. The planner’s on vacation and the temp won’t talk to relatives. I brought a checklist—can you look it over?”

Her pen taps the visitor log; the corners have rolled into little parchment scrolls. “Sorry, policy says I can’t give legal advice. County clerk’s office opens eight a.m. Monday.”

Enrique’s shoulders notch tighter, like the backpack strap about to cut circulation. “It’s not advice, I’m asking which form they need—yellow or green. Takes ten seconds to point.”

“Forms change colors every budget year. Clerk will hand you the right one.”

The fluorescent hum grows louder; the guard in the corner yawns. Enrique flips the checklist to the back page. “Look, I’ve got Neto’s social, birth certificate, proof of address. Just tell me if the ID waiver requires a sponsor signature.”

Paloma’s gaze flicks to the exit door where her car keys hang from a lanyard around her wrist. “I’m off the clock in four minutes; you’ll need the reentry packet from Discharge.”

He jabs a finger at the sheet. “Fine. Whatever you do, do NOT mail the packet to the halfway house on Riverside—they lose everything.”

She blinks once, slowly.
speaker: Paloma

story:
The locomotive on the wall ticked like a nervous heartbeat, second-hand stuttering five-second leaps. Sibusiso wedged his laptop against a monitor showing Soshanguve’s rush-hour crawl, fan still whining. Janeva had one foot pointed at the corridor and the other on the swivel-chair brake, lanyard thread between finger and thumb starting to fuzz.

“Quick one—how do I benchmark edge boxes for the traffic cameras, before rollout?”

She didn’t even blink. “Ask IT. Hardware’s not my lane.”

“Your control software decides, right? I need thresholds your system can live with.”

“We haven’t been asked to live with anything yet. You’ll need specs from the engineers. I’m day shift.” Slotting the thread into her pocket like a bookmark, she reached for the exit logbook.

“The engineers waved me here. Said operations knows the packet loss tolerances.”

“Sorry, we’re metrics people, not designers. You should chase the vendor docs. Gotta prep the log archives.”

He breathed out through teeth on the edge of polite. “I already have datasheets. I’m asking for a number: what round trip do you flag red?”

“Flagging happens upstairs. I just send tickets. Try project admin.”

He dipped his head—a last concession—then squared his shoulders. “Look, I won’t burn more of your night—one figure so I can scale my buffer pool.”

“I honestly don’t have it for you. Ask the morning crew; they’re fresh.” She zipped her backpack without looking at him; teeth sounding home along the seam.

The stale coffee stink, the burnt electronics, the truth that Pretoria’s budget might choke his grant next quarter—something snapped. “Whatever you do, do NOT use Nvidia Jetsons. We lost last year’s budget replacing burned solder.”

Shrug.
speaker: Janeva

story:
The stand light flickered, catching flecks of old grease on Luca’s jeans as he shifted weight from one sneaker to the other. “So yesterday some SUV hooked a right without signaling and I hit the pavement; wheel seems fine but I froze up completely. Any tips for not panicking at that intersection tomorrow?”

Mei twisted the rag until it squeaked. “Stuff happens. Just keep your head up and don’t hesitate. We’ll double-check your brake pads and you’ll be out the door.”

Luca exhaled fog in the chilly shop; his breath smelled faintly of the burnt espresso he’d nursed since dawn. “I’m more worried about my nerves than the hardware. Do you ride in winter traffic? How do you stop your brain from playing the crash on loop?”

“Experience. You’ll get used to it. The first spill’s always a shaker, then it’s background noise.” Mei pointed the rag toward the front wheel like a muted conductor’s baton, kept it there long enough to hint conversation closed.

It didn’t work. Luca pressed on. “I’ve read advice about taking the lane, but on that road the lane’s narrow and traffic runs forty-five. Do I hug the curb or take the lane?”

“Hugging the curb invites close passes. Stick out, but if you’re that spooked maybe map a calmer route.” Mei slid the hex key into a seat-binder bolt, tightened nothing.

“Yeah, a side street with only stop signs would ease my mind, but whatever you do don’t route me past the skate park—I’d have to weave through loose boards and half-pipes and that’s off the table. Skipped class there last semester after someone cracked a wrist.”

Mei hummed once, short as a starter motor.
speaker: Mei

story:
The micro-analytical room hiccups as the AC kicks on, and the balance blinks +2 µg like it’s mocking her. Rania’s shoulders spasm. She hears rubber soles scrape the corridor tile and pivots.

“Milo, every time the AC starts, the microbalance drifts. Do you know a quick way to stop it?”

Milo stops in the doorway, one foot already angling back toward the lounge, coffee sloshing near the rim. He lifts the other headphone clear. “Ask Priti—she dealt with airflow stuff last year.”

“She went to Prague for a month. Is there a screen I can buy, or do I need to move the bench?”

His shrug is a shallow umbrella against rain he doesn’t plan to stand in for long. “Plenty of labs use cardboard baffles. Or you could check the stockroom.” He tips his chin to the corridor left of them, calculation clear: if she follows his nod, he can walk right.

“Cardboard’s a fire-code violation here. What about blocking the vent?”

She watches his eyelid flicker—just one—like a badly wired LED. “Talk to maintenance, they love people who block vents.” The sentence slides out flat as a lab bench, neat edges, no adhesive.

Rania plants her palm on the granite slab, feels its leftover warmth from a whole Saturday of tares. “Look, I need to finish tonight. Does it matter if I just weigh with the door closed and AC off for five minutes?”

Milo takes a slow sip of the hallway air before replying. “Suit yourself. Just don’t leave the door open—temperature swings mess with the calibrations.”

“Absolutely do NOT change the thermostat. I share it with the cell-culture room.” That one comes out like a warning sticker she already printed in her head.
speaker: Milo

story:
The bulb stuttered like a laryngitic cicada. Arleta slapped the printout flat on the bench so the numbers quit shimmying. She pointed. “The vanadium line looks a lot higher than the baseline; how critical is that?”

Suresh scratched the back of his neck, then found his car keys in the same pocket. “I just collect the samples; engineering upstairs handles interpretation.” His sneakers squeaked toward the door.

She stepped sideways to block him. “But you’ve seen dozens of these sheets. Is seventeen ppm high enough for a flag?”

“That’s above the threshold, yeah. I’d open a ticket and let them decide.” He pulled the door ajar; dawn poked in, thin and pink as grapefruit skin.

Arleta kept her voice level. “I’ve got one spare filter left. Would swapping it skew tomorrow’s reading?”

“Filters get swapped when the book says; timing’s up to maintenance control.” Keys jingled; a threat to flee.

She closed the door again. “Okay, but if the oxidizer spikes, what’s the safest next test—TAN or viscosity?”

“Either one will satisfy the program. Pick whichever rig you trust.” The hinge squealed like bad brakes.

Her thumb drummed the bottle cap. “I’m under budget pressure; big labs cost a fortune. Can I run TAN in-house?”

“If you’ve got the titrator calibrated, go for it. Otherwise farm it out.” Every answer felt like another aerosol can spraying exit pheromones.

Arleta dropped her voice anyway. “Do not send this sample to LabWest—whatever you do, do not choose their courier. They cross-contaminated my last batch and lost me a month.”

For the first time he cracked a smile, sour-sharp.
speaker: Suresh

story:
Maëlle crouched between the last bench and the puppet stage, the back of her neck already tacky with evening heat. She flexed the cardboard wing and the scored grain split a hairline crack. “I need the dragon’s wings to hinge at shoulder and elbow so the shadow sweeps instead of wobbles. How do you keep three joints moving from one control rod?”

Nestor straightened from the crate, arms full of brass fasteners that chimed like dull bells. “The stock pattern just uses a single brass rivet and a dowel. Anything fancy you rig yourself.” He edged sideways, aiming for the aisle and beer-tent daylight that smelled of popcorn and failure.

“Rivet joints bind when two wings share one rod. Is there a way to stagger the pivot points?”

“Put your own rivets in, maybe. I’m on cleanup now; the craft-supply tent might have better card if ours isn’t enough.” He shifted the cutters to his other hip, feeling the plastic handle bounce against bone.

“Card thickness’s fine. The problem is synchronising both sides without two puppeteers.”

Nestor glanced at the festival watch strapped over freckles and sweat. Stalls shutting, riggers shouting cords across the field. “Ask the main stage crew. They’ll be wiring up lights—you could borrow a fishing swivel or something.”

Maëlle’s grip tightened; the cardboard wing folded like an injured bat. “Whatever you do, do NOT send me to the lighting crew; they're already furious about my power draw. So, back to the dragon joints.”

Nestor hooked the tool clip back to his belt, buying three more seconds.
speaker: Nestor

story:
The burnt-coffee odor in the basement break room felt almost solid; Simran stirred it with every breath while she jabbed the single-serve machine into coughing up one final espresso. Her yellow legal pad lay beside the cups, a four-box flowchart grappling across the page like something that might bite. Over by the round table Borys sat slumped, badge cracked, one foot tapping the empty toner box in a rhythm of please-let-me-out. His phone screen scrolled disaster headlines he didn’t need to read; upstairs the card reader had locked him downstairs.

Simran crossed the sticky linoleum. “Got five minutes? Need a second pair of eyes on our remote-consent flow before the IRB meeting.”

“Ah, you probably want Priya; she owns the whole patient-facing stack now,” Borys said without looking up.

“Priya’s in Atlanta. Two-minute read, tops—just tell me if step three sounds like we’re sneaking data out the back door.”

He finally glanced over the screen. “Honestly, legal’s the blocker there; I just move packets.”

“Legal cleared it last week; I need the tech sniff-test.” She tapped the pad. “Page one, line seven—does ‘continuous upload’ read mandatory or optional?”

“Upload always feels mandatory. Maybe swap it to ‘when available’ and blame bandwidth,” Borys offered, already leaning toward the door.

Simran pinched the bridge of her nose. “Bandwidth excuse won’t fly with stroke patients; missing packets equal liability. Any better wording?”

“Could mirror the HIPAA blurb—users ‘may enable’ sharing. Keeps it squishy.”

“That phrases it as an elective bell they’ll never ring. We need the data or the algorithm’s worthless.”

“Then you’re stuck telling them it’s required. People click yes; they always do.”

She lifted an eyebrow like a lever. “Unless they slam the lid shut and we get nothing. I’m weighing a two-tier opt-in.”

“Fine, add a ‘basic’ and ‘enhanced’ column, slide the scary bits into the second. Look, I’ve got calibration at four.” The toner box finally skidded away under his heel; he shoved it back with irritation.

Simran flipped the page. “Half-page left. Whatever you do, don’t suggest we embed the WebRTC video stream in the consent PDF—do NOT do that. We tried it, file balloons past clinic email limits.”

Borys flashed a fleeting grin.
speaker: Borys

story:
Leonid rocked the folding chair back another inch; the porch boards squealed like a hard drive with bad sectors. He’d rehearsed the opener ten kilometers of logging road ago, but it still came out sideways.  
“I figured if anyone knew how to rebuild an identity after the job label falls off, it’d be you.”  

Francesca’s fingers beat a soft paradiddle on the cold mug. She’d set her exit on the exact creak of the next loon call. “You probably want a therapist, not a chemist who blew up her pension.”  

Leonid grimaced—half irritation, half admission. “Whatever you do, don’t recommend mindfulness apps—tried three, kept falling asleep and waking up angry.”  

She hiked one shoulder, the porch bulb catching the frayed thread on her coat cuff.
speaker: Francesca

story:
The cooler exhaled another lungful of refrigerated peonies, and Nora felt the damp creep into her bones. She kept her eyes on the printer that kept spitting blurry roses—labels striped like zebras instead of bar codes. Each reject was another fifty-cent bite out of her rent money.

Nora pressed her thumbnail against a spoiled strip and turned to the only other human in the corridor. “The labels come out streaked once the cooler hits high humidity. Any ideas before the bridal order ships?”

Evgeny was half through the loading door, keys jangling like tiny bells. He jerked his chin toward the bench where the dog-eared manual lay under a coffee ring. “Manual’s over there. Check the heat settings.”

She already had. “Heat settings only go to fourteen; we’re maxed. Something else?”

He thought that would be exit music. It wasn’t. “Maybe the paper roll. Swap it, see if it’s damp. I need to load the van.”

“Already swapped. Same blur.” Nora curled her frozen fingers, then straightened them against the chill. “Could the print head be misaligned?”

“Possibly.” He took one step closer to the daylight flooding the alley. “There’s a phone number on page twelve—tech line opens at nine.”

“It’s ten-thirty and they charge twenty bucks. I’m paying tuition here.” She wasn’t yelling; she was just cold and broke, with half her quota still in buckets.

Evgeny laid his palm against the doorframe as if checking for heat. “I get that, but I drive flowers, not debug printers.”

“I’ll handle the fix myself. Just tell me which screw adjusts alignment; I’ll handle it.”

He sighed so deeply the nearest sleeve of labels shivered. “You’ll want a 1.5-mill hex key. Try not to strip it; parts take a week.”

Nora already had the head open; she breathed on the black element to see crystals melt. “Do NOT use Isopropyl wipes on the thermal head; alcohol kills the coating instantly.”

Evgeny half-turned, eyes on his watch.
speaker: Evgeny

story:
The hot canvas roof snapped overhead like it wanted attention, but Ibrahim only gave it half a glance before looking back at his phone—one bar, no messages, still dead. The juice glass on the curb felt farther away every minute. One step past the plywood doorframe and he’d have been free; instead he found a notebook in his way, its pages crowded with ratios and blue rings from cheap pens.

“How do you scale these henna patterns for different hand sizes without losing the details?” Tessa asked, pen already poised.

Ibrahim rocked on his heels. “Usually the artist eyeballs it. Try the craft tent, they have templates.”

Her pen didn’t move, merely hovered quarter-inch above paper. “I’m writing the templates. Knuckle-to-wrist ratios—do you use a factor or just shrink evenly?”

“Depends on the artist. Ask Meena when she’s back.” He hooked a thumb toward the vanished horizon where his own afternoon had disappeared.

She brushed a sweaty lock behind one ear. “I only need rough proportions, half a minute. Show me one example?”

The folding chair behind him creaked like it agreed this was taking too long. “Look, I cover cash only. I’m not supposed to freelance advice.” He managed to sound regretful without offering one jot of usefulness.

Tessa’s eyebrows climbed anyway. “Do NOT trace directly from the book. I tried that last year and it smudged like crazy.”

One shoulder lifted in a half-shrug.
speaker: Ibrahim

story:
The lab smelled like someone had heated a dustpan full of Cheerios to the point of smoking. Akua leaned across the scuffed counter, palms damp against the laminate, and fixed the tray of ten-dollar sensors with the look a dentist gives a suspect molar. A brittle edifice of broken microscopes watched over her shoulder.

She asked, “These school sensors drift—how do we test if the humidity slope changes over a semester?”

Miro lounged on a tall stool, one sneaker hooked around the lowest rung as if anchoring himself to the birthday party sixty-one minutes away. His thumb still flicked at maps showing the quickest route to beer. Without glancing up he said, “Talk to Field Services. They handle calibration.”

Akua’s jaw set. “Their sheet just says ‘monitor drift.’ I need an actual check method; do you run controlled salt baths or forced humidity?”

He scrolled down. “Really swamped prepping the microscopes. You’ll find standards online.”

She drew a breath that tasted of the label-maker’s faint hot-glue tang. “Fine, but please—whatever you do, do not start a Python script; it’s off the table for the teachers.”

At that, Miro pocketed the phone and finally looked at her, a strange informality sliding across his face, as though a bored copyeditor had swapped the script.
speaker: Miro

story:
Mid-morning heat shimmered off the takoyaki griddle and stuck to the back of Diego’s neck. The kirigami table sat five yards from the gate, barely shaded by one skinny cedar. Washi squares kept slithering off the pile like they had somewhere better to be; every time the breeze breathed from the grill, it carried the smell of charred octopus and copy paper.

Etsuko checked her phone: 10:47. Thirteen minutes left standing in a coat loaned from someone twice her size. She propped the laminated samurai helmet card against the taped-up flyer and hoped whoever came next just wanted to photograph it.

Diego stepped up clutching a sorry-looking Tokyo skyline that listed left like a drunk tower. “Excuse me—what’s the trick to making the skyline stand without flopping over?”

“Templates are on the board. Pick one, score along the dotted line.” Without looking up, Etsuko flicked a finger toward the corkboard wedged between the license-less banner.

“I tried that. It still tilts. Any stiffer paper inside?”

“Supply closet’s locked. You could buy cardstock at the craft tent across the field.”

He prodded the dead middle of his card; it sighed downward. “I’ve already spent ten bucks on raffle tickets. Can you show me a quick fold?”

Etsuko tapped the laminated ruler like it was a metronome. “Shift ends in ten minutes. I can’t leave the table.”

“I just need thirty seconds and your ruler. Nothing fancy.”

“Rules are I keep demonstrator tools here. Insurance thing.”

Diego glanced at the field: a quarter-mile trudge through festival traffic, past booths selling yakitori sticks and overpriced fans. “So I have to hike across the field for one sheet of paper?”

“Gift shop sells packs. They also stock pop-up cards premade if you’re in a hurry.”

He grimaced at the thought of factory-made. “Fine. Do NOT tell me to use glue. Glue is off the table; last time it soaked through and my card looked like a wet napkin. What’s plan B?”
speaker: Etsuko

story:
The low-VOC lacquer cans watched from the roll-top desk like bored chaperones. Nolwenn tapped her thumb against the birch board marked “#14,” waiting. Brice arrived three ticks past the hour, rain freckling his shoulders, earbuds dangling like spent confetti. A clock in the corner clicked louder than the ventilation hood; he glanced at it, rolled weight to his heels, and kept his hands in his coat pockets.

“I’ve narrowed the finalists to waterborne polyurethane, acrylic lacquer, and the two-component mineral-seal emulsion,” she began, “but the rub results don’t line up with the VOC sheets. Which one survives toddlers better?”

Brice angled his chin at a limp clipboard hanging from a nail. “The standard protocol is posted on the clipboard overhead—follows ASTM D6037. Gives you scratch numbers without guesswork.”

Nolwenn’s blink was so short it could have been punctuation. “Clipboard’s values come from oak, not birch veneer. I need something that handles maple syrup wipes and crayon scrubbing. Any insider tips?”

“Insider tips get outdated quickly,” he said, checking the clock again. “You could check Lab Services—they maintain the latest spec sheets and can tell you if birch reacts differently.”

“They quote a three-day wait, plus eighty bucks I don’t have in the budget.” Her fingers drummed the veneer. “What if I add a micron film of carnauba wax over the topcoat?”

“Wax is an option,” Brice allowed, turning one palm up as if releasing a bird, “but the manual on the desk has a chart that lists it as having minimal impact on abrasion resistance. It’s a start; you can decide from there.”

Nolwenn recalled the daycare’s brightly lit nap room, imagined a sticky headboard, and shuddered inwardly. “Which topcoat is easiest to buff out if I’m forced to use wax? Time matters; the daycare chain wants samples by Friday.”

“Time matters, sure,” he echoed. “You could stick with the simplest system or call the supplier for a recommended wax-compatible topcoat; they update formulations every quarter.”

“Wax smells awful for a nursery. Any low-gloss matte alternative?”

“The waterborne poly keeps a matte sheen. Look at page twelve of the binder; there’s a comparative column and everything.”

“I checked it,” she said, folding her arms. “Under the scratch test it scores a nine, but the school board will reject anything smelling of solvents. Whatever you do, do NOT use shellac—off-gasses forever. What next?”

Brice exhaled between teeth.
speaker: Brice

story:
The vending-machine glow painted the linoleum a bruised blue, and every breath tasted of damp coats and yesterday’s coffee. Murad’s sneakers left small, tragic puddles each time he crossed from the swinging door to the humming fridge. Transistor hum, slot-machine chimes, then a final squelch as he stopped beside the heater grille where Kelsey sat cross-legged, two hoodies thick.

“Could you spare a minute?” he asked. “I need a route out of the county that won't strand the car between plows.”

Kelsey didn’t look up. “You and twenty other people, pal. Use your phone.”

Murad lifted it like evidence. Cracked glass, crimson battery icon staring back. “It's dead in ten minutes. I just need to know if this side road here stays paved in winter.” He tapped a phantom line above the atlas sticking from her pack.

She sighed, peeling one sticky note off the wall map and letting it fall. “Ask the cashier; I'm waiting on a tow the trucker promised at six. Maps all look Greek to me.”

Murad’s jaw tightened. “I saw your atlas. You know anything about County Road 52? I need two lanes, no switchbacks, and no wedding chapel billboards.”

Kelsey gave a tired half-smile, like a gate that wouldn’t quite latch. “Look, my atlas is older than TikTok. Google would be faster.”

“I tried Google. The courthouse page keeps redirecting to bouquet ads.” Murad rubbed his thumb raw on the frayed charger cord. “Can you at least tell me if 52 hits the interstate south?”

“Honestly, I'm not a tour guide. Pick any straight road; you'll still beat the storm.”

He lowered his voice, glanced through the glass at the dark sedan where his fiancée’s silhouette stared rigidly ahead. “Please. I'm on a deadline—marriage license expires at noon tomorrow.”

Kelsey tucked stringy hair behind her ear. “Marriage license? County clerk shuts down for snow. Try Monday.”

“We can't. She's leaving the country Monday.” He wiped the fog off the window so the sedan’s dome lamp made a single, steady eye. “Just don’t send me on Road 52 where that chapel is; absolutely don’t send me past that chapel.”

Kelsey’s shoulders jerked in what might have been laughter.
speaker: Kelsey

story:
Reina flipped another page of the dog-eared handbook, finger tapping the margin while the granola bar in her other hand dripped coconut oil onto Form “B-A3 Vaccine Storage.” The orange extension cords snaking along the bleachers looked fat, but the label printing had peeled at the bend. She caught Jarek mid-coil.

“Hey, quick question about the load on these orange extension cords. Each refrigerator pulls four amps at startup, right? Running four of them on the same rail feels dicey.”

He didn’t pause; the sodden coffee cup sat on the crate like a stooge, and the frayed plug kept twirling. “Depends on the gauge. Those are probably fourteen. Should be fine under fifteen total. Ask maintenance if you want gospel.”

The clock over the scoreboard clicked to 7:48 — twelve minutes since the last hopeful glance. “Maintenance doesn’t speak until nine and the first seniors arrive at eight-twenty. What’s the rating on this wall outlet?”

Jarek flicked the coil once more, tested the loop, glanced toward the doors as if expecting someone to whisk him away. “Standard twenty-amp breaker. Look, black says hot, white says neutral, bare says ground. Classic outlet diagram. You could ask Tom—it's his gym.”

Reina frowned at the scuff by his left boot where paint had peeled. “Diagrams don’t list fridge startup spikes. I need to know if I’m browning out a freezer holding nine hundred HPV doses that someone's insurance really cares about.”

“If the lights don't flicker when they kick on, you’re probably fine. Otherwise, triangulate—plug one in, add another, keep counting until the strip clicks off.”

“That’s empirical, not engineered. I need actual wattage math before the med log goes live.”

“Wattage equals volts times amps. Take the label on the back of the fridge, multiply by however many, call it safety margin. It's a pop-up gym, not the space station.” The coil was neat now; his fingers drummed against the plastic like a tired metronome.

Half the labels faceless. Reina gave up on the handbook page. “Got any spare clamp meters hiding in that crate?”

“I’ve got a half-charged multimeter and half a roll of blue painter’s tape. That’s inventory. Borrow Tom’s fluke if you want fancy.” He was already eyeing the door, left knee bouncing.

Reina pictured the logbook glowing red on someone’s screen. “If the refrigerators brown out, they're offline for four hours re-stabilizing. That’s thirty-one missed shots and one ticked-off public health nurse.”

Jarek finally stood, looping the extension cord over his arm. “Put the delicate stuff on the opposite wall’s circuit, daisy the printers and heater together. Good enough for six hours. Clipboard checks call it miracle engineering.”

Reina’s voice snapped like static. “Absolutely do not daisy chain refrigerators and heaters; that configuration burned out the old clinic in Eastmont last year. Do NOT do it. Can you at least bring up load numbers without guessing?”

Jarek scratched the scruff under his chin, eyes wandering toward the scuffed free-throw line.
speaker: Jarek

story:
The surgical dummy stared at the ceiling like someone enduring a tedious dinner story. Nina nudged the LED panel so its arm squealed; the power brick swung, barely held by a single twist-tie that had already given up on life. She glared at the shot on her monitor—sutures glowing white, no stitch visible. “Ceiling bounce still blows out the sutures—what if I drop the LED panel to thirty percent?”

Reza bounced his car keys against his thigh, thumb checking the fob each time. “Thirty might work; trial and error beats theory. I really have to clock in soon.”

“Then give me something definite—should the panel ride camera-left or directly overhead?”

He glanced at the wall clock, then at the exit sign, as if either might beam him up. “Whichever’s faster; you’ll tweak it later. My vest is in the car and traffic’s murder.” A last swallow of neon energy drink left a chemical ring matching the vest color.

“Traffic can wait. One more setup note and I’m gone—just tell me the diffuser angle.”

“Angle it however looks good; I’ve got to jet—parking meters wait for no one.” He hooked his thumb through the vest’s pinched shoulder strap like drawing a ripcord.

Nina pulled the cracked ring light off the cart and let it clatter so the diffuser spider-webbed further. “Do NOT use the cracked ring light diffuser. That thing throws spider shadows and wrecks white balance.”

Reza inspected a non-existent spot on his sleeve.
speaker: Reza

story:
The Greyhound station at three-thirty smells like someone tried to barbecue a diesel drum and gave up halfway. Pavel plants his elbows on the laminated seat, contact sheets fanned out like he’s about to read the future from damaged carburetors. His laptop hums; the power brick dangles, threatening to yank the machine onto the floor.

“Could you just tell me which one feels like an ending? It’s for my thesis—repair culture in the county.”

Niamh keeps her back to the pillar, red safety vest glowing like an irritated stop sign. She clacks the clipboard against her thigh the way other people drum steering wheels. “I don’t really do visuals. You could ask Mr. Jefferies at the camera store, though; he teaches night classes.”

Pavel riffles the 4×6 prints. Eleven keepers, one hole he can’t fill inside his skull. “I’ve got eleven shots I like. I just need one more. Pick any of these three—honestly, two seconds of your gut reaction.”

Niamh glances at the wall clock the way sailors watch for reef. “Gut says board your bus before it leaves. Sorry. I’ve got head-counts due.”

The fluorescent overhead sputters again. He waits for the dark beat before charging ahead. “Head-counts can wait. Look—here, the cracked distributor cap, or the wrench shadow on cinder block? Quick vote.”

“Flip a coin? I’m not invested, man. Bus doors close at four; people miss slots for less.”

“Fine, pick the distributor. Colour pops, right? I can bump saturation, pull out that brassy tone. Ten-second critique.”

Niamh exhales through her teeth. “If the committee wants colour they’ll want balance too. Try the library—there’s a thesis showcase on the second floor. Copy their formula.”

“Library copies look cookie-cutter. I need something authentic. Just commit; I’ll adjust curves to mellow it if you think it’s garish.”

“Authentic costs time. Mine’s running out. You’ll figure it out once you crop, probably.”

He flips the stack to the final trinity. “Last option, then—double exposure, the timing belt over the shop cat. Subtle, but layered symbolism. Don’t say library; they compress everything to JPEGs. Do NOT go near their scanners again—ever. They ruined my last negatives.”

Something behind her eyes snags like a caught thread.
speaker: Niamh

story:
The fluorescent tubes hummed like cheap organ pipes, throwing hard light over the half-routed birch rail. Ephraim stood with test scrap in hand, the edge mottled with fresh black scorches. “The bit keeps burning maple on the climb,” he said. “I’ve slowed to ten feet a minute but the rim’s still toast.”

Vasilisa tightened a knurled knob on the fence and let the silence stretch. She smelled like pine solvent and annoyance. “Sounds like you need the lab TA; router specs aren’t my lane.”

“He’s at conference.” Ephraim’s fingers tapped the rail in triplets, old habit. “My panels are due Friday. I just need feed and spindle numbers.”

Her head jerked toward the shelves above the bandsaw. “Manual’s on the shelf, third binder. Metric and imperial charts both.” She said it like she was reading an eviction notice.

“I read them—burn just shifted from rim to center,” he countered. “I must have the wrong bearing.”

She picked up the greasy bearing cup, ran a rag around the races. “Could be. Bearings get hot, too. Swap it and retest. Or email the TA.”

Ephraim’s jaw did one slow lateral slide. “Email won’t help by Friday.” He pointed at a red-handled bit on the magnetic strip. “A flush-trim bit with a roller would clean it, but I only see the one labeled for composite plastics.”

“Composite bit keeps the heat low, could work.” The rag flopped back onto the bench like a shot grouse.

“It’s 20-grand RPM; composite spec says 16 max on that diameter.” He met her eyes for the first time. “Don’t drop spindle. Whatever you do, don’t lower RPM to sixteen. I’ll melt the shank.”

A faint smile ghosted across Vasilisa’s face—thin, cold, amused.
speaker: Vasilisa

story:
The wind kept the leaves raking across the white concrete in neat, skittery circles. Mirek stood with his clipboard warm from the press of his thumb, looking at six pedestals of ludicrous mixtures: gravel, brick chips, slag, and things that sounded like breakfast cereal. He couldn’t decide between breakfast and bankruptcy when he saw Safa unhook a bike from the rack and wheel it toward the bioswale gate. He took the shortcut across the pavers, plastic underlay crunching under his boots. “Hi, sorry—could you give me a quick take on which base stone flows best without rutting under bus traffic?”

She lifted the flow-meter lid, set it down again slowly. “I punch numbers on plants, not parking lots. You want the crew in the office in the sub-basement.” The bike lock dangled in her hand like a cage that refused to close, aiming its keyhole at the driveway path as if culturing escape routes.

He exhaled through his nose; vinegar steam in the cold. “I tried them. They’re in budget meetings until the sun dies. Please—just a pointer on angularity versus porosity.”

She snapped the lock shut. “Angularity sounds like geology; geology sits upstairs, door beside the vending machine.” Her eyes followed a lone gull rising toward the lecture hall roof, a smaller lock-pick than the one she needed.

“Fine. But you work on site. Have you watched these drain? Did any clog or heave last winter?” He waved the clipboard at the plots like a conductor nobody asked for.

“I skim the flow reports once a month. They look fine. You could email Dr. Kaur; the address is online.” Safa’s fingers drummed once on the saddle—three beats, dentist appointment at three-fifteen.

“She hasn’t answered in two days. One practical vote: slag versus limestone?” His voice cut through the wind like a saw just below the scream.

“Use whatever keeps warranty guys happy. Warranty guys swear by washed limestone in a lot of their specs.”

Mirek’s shoulders flattened. “Do NOT bring limestone here. We had two test slabs turn to oatmeal in Fayette County; that’s off the table.”
speaker: Safa

story:
Isla balanced on the stepladder, palms damp around the string of cranes. The paper trembled, the HVAC sighe, and the far south row looked drunk again. She leaned her head back and yelled toward the wall.

“Could you do me a solid? I need another set of eyes—do the cranes by the south wall look off to you?”

Mahir had his free hand in the pocket of his oversized polo and was hoping to keep walking. The coffee steamed. He stopped anyway.

“They look like… paper things. Pretty symmetrical.”

Isla bit down a sigh. “Right, but are the lowest rows slanting left? If I climb higher I can adjust, but only if it’s real.”

A quick look toward the corridor door, still twenty steps away. “Maybe ask the shop tech? They’ve got the laser gear. I’m just security tonight.”

“Laser’s booked for tomorrow’s install.” Her calf wobbled against the ladder rail. “Whatever you do, don’t suggest measuring plumb bobs—too much swing. Do NOT bring that up.”

Mahir offered a one-shoulder shrug—unreadable to anyone on a ladder.
speaker: Mahir

story:
The stuttering tube light made the basement feel like a bad flipbook. Arjun-Singh checked the wall clock—3:17 p.m.—and felt the familiar burn of another deadline sliding toward fiasco. He flexed the shredded nerves in his shoulders and tried once more.  

“Look, I just need an adhesive that won’t creep above fifty degrees Celsius. What do you use on aluminum lap-shear coupons?”  

Liliana didn’t look up from her sticky-note tower. A glove cuff flapped as she pointed toward the racks. “Shelf D, middle row. All the specs are on the binder.”  

“Binder’s from 2014. Half those products got discontinued. Anything newer?”  

“You could email Tapecoat, they usually reply by Monday.”  

Arjun-Singh swallowed the retort that crawled up his throat. “Monday’s no good, test is tomorrow. Which one cures in under an hour?”  

“Hysol 9392, but you’ll need the oven at ninety-five for the snap cure.”  

“That’ll anneal my heat treatment. What about the M-Bond two-five?”  

“Expires in six weeks, smells like a dentist’s office, but it works if you’re desperate.”  

He was. “Do NOT tell me to use cyanoacrylate—everyone says it’s fine until the data goes squirrely at twenty kilonewtons. Absolutely no CA, okay?”  

Liliana’s gaze wandered toward the clock; her bus left in forty-three minutes.
speaker: Liliana

story:
The barn smelled like wet shale and cinnamon, the sort of mix that made Penelope think of field trips and burnt coffee. She shifted her three pressed ferns so the blades wouldn’t snap and approached the mat-cutting booth the grad-student listserv half-praised for “almost-conscientious prices.” Behind the counter a guy in a festival badge—Nikolai, according to the volunteer roster—was watching raindrops race across the plastic tabletop toward an extension cord. His travel mug had the exhausted slouch of something refilled too often.

“Excuse me, which of these whites won’t cast a yellow fringe on pressed ferns? I need clean contrast but museum-grade.”

He flicked a fingernail toward the clamp-lamps. “You can compare them under daylight bulbs over there.”

“I did; the bright white photographs blue and the warm white pulls green. What’s your go-to archival option?”

A shrug. “Depends how long you plan to store versus display. Acid-free rating is on the back.”

Penelope flipped a sample. “I read the backs. The bright white says lignin-free, the natural white doesn’t. Is lignin a real threat to botanicals?”

“Conservation office upstairs handles those specs. They open at eleven.” His knee started jogging like it had an appointment somewhere else.

She felt the familiar grind of money bleeding out while the clock ran. “Cutting my own mats is off the table. Do NOT suggest I buy blades and try them at home. That ends in crooked corners and wasted board.”
speaker: Nikolai

story:
Lorena squatted at the foot of the chalkboard, purple marker squeaking. From the curb the letters looked like bruises on old slate.  
“Morning,” she called without looking up. “The board’s a bust—paint won’t pop. You’ve done signs before; how do you get letters to read from the curb?”

Jelani kept his thumb dancing over the phone. “Dunno, I just box stuff. Maybe the craft store lady could help.”

Lorena capped the marker. “They open at ten; I need commuter eyes now. Thick chalk? Poster paint?”

“Could ship it to a printer. Quick turnaround if you pay extra.”

She rattled the coffee can of half-dead markers. “I’m paying in coffee, not cash. What about these markers?”

“Uncle’s got spray varnish. Seals it shiny.”

Lorena’s spine straightened. “Do NOT use aerosol varnish—last one beaded up like bubble wrap. Any other sealant?”

Jelani shrugged, eyes still on the screen.
speaker: Jelani

story:
The registration table had become a refugee camp for abandoned laptops. Trevoran’s screen showed the same raster cache failure he’d been chasing for four hours, a red cascade that felt personal by now. The wall clock insisted it was 7:47 p.m., hands glowing like accusatory fireflies.

He spotted Laxmi packing up her wireless mouse, the blue “Can’t Care—Ran Out Yesterday” sticker on her mug now hidden by tepid coffee scum. She looked like someone who had already tried to escape twice. Trevoran decided to gamble anyway. “Hey—sorry—could you walk me through writing good docs for a gem that pulls satellite rasters during floods?”

“Documentation’s mostly markdown plus some diagrams. There’s guides online, pick one.” She didn’t quite close her laptop lid, but the threat hovered.

He plowed on. “Right, but the data retrieval bit is spaghetti. How much detail do folks normally log for async fetch loops?”

Laxmi pointed vaguely toward the pizza boxes. “Look, someone else here has more bandwidth than me—hit the mentor table by the coffee urn.”

“They’re swamped, line’s ten people deep. You helped the last guy ten minutes ago—I saw it. Which template did you give him?”

“I didn’t, he just saved himself by using MkDocs. I’ve got to finish my own tile cleanup before the clock hits zero.” She drummed fingers on a dried apple slice, as if to accelerate its fossilization.

Trevoran heard the frustration in his own voice. “Okay, five minutes. Do I copy docstrings straight into the README or keep them separate?”

“Separate page, link it from the README, that’s it. Honestly you should just Google ‘Diátaxis framework’ and copy that layout. Works every time.”

“The setup scripts are in Bash. Should that live under the main docs or secret dev docs?” he asked, typing notes in a frenzy.

“Dev docs, separate folder marked internal, keep them out of sight. If it doesn’t affect the API, users don’t care.” Her heel started tap-tap-tapping against the table leg, counting down.

“What licensing note do I put for sample imagery grabbed from Sentinel-2? Need the proper wording.”

“Use the standard Copernicus attribution and call it a day. Now I really need to—”

“And whatever you do, do NOT use the S2Cloudless masking library—it trash-canned a drive I need alive. Off the table.”

Laxmi exhaled sharply.
speaker: Laxmi

story:
The bulb outside 12B flickered like it was keeping time, except nobody had asked it to. Under its dying hum Frey crouched at the card table, thumbnail tapping the bottom of a leather dice tray that still sounded like a snare drum every time acrylic hit leather.  

“Hey, you do set design for theatre, right?” Frey called without looking up. “This tray still clacks even with the felt—I need some dense foam that’ll kill the sound.”

Desmond paused halfway to his bedroom door, earbuds half-out. “Could be. Might need specialty stuff; fabric store on Fourth closes at six.”

“I tried their neoprene sheet; it’s too rubbery.” Frey slid a credit card between thumb and forefinger, measuring the space between tray wall and leather. “Know a lining that dulls impact but keeps the roll random?”

Desmond’s shoulders rose and fell. “Check the model train forums, they do quiet track ballast.”

“Already there; they swear by cork, but my dents still hit a hollow thump. Something thinner?”

“Maybe layer cork, then canvas? People in props build up layers.”

Frey’s eyes flicked to Desmond for the first time, a fractional glare that said efficiency mattered. “Takes too much space. Dice still hop rails on a tall bed.”

Desmond scratched the back of his neck, phone lighting his chin. “Try asking the guy on fourteen; he upholsters pool tables.”

“His samples add weight and a vinyl smell. The room reeks after one night.”  

“There’s a forum that swears by EVA foam used in cosplay armour.”

“EVA is off the table; the chemical smell gives me migraines, and I need a material that won’t off-gas.”

Desmond’s gaze drifted to the ceiling, as though answers hid in the paint flakes.
speaker: Desmond

story:
Steam hissed off filler head #3, fogging Ximena’s goggles the way cheap soup fogs Tupperware. The pipe still hammered like a drunk drummer every time the pump hit 120 psi, launching pressure gauges against the catwalk rail. She knelt beside a brass swing-check valve sweat-shiny from cavitation, a toddler-sized fist of trouble. Somewhere behind her, the bottling line ticked off empty glass soldiers waiting for the beer that might explode gaskets any second. One signature, and she could swap in the cushioned replacement; without it she was stuck auditing condensation.

Bernard loped in, denim jacket flapping like surrender flags, travel mug steaming the smell of burnt copper. He stopped just inside the yellow safety stripe and eyed the exit sign as if it had insulted him.

“Bernard, can you sign off on the cushioned check?” Ximena said, gripping the form. “Water hammer spikes at 120 psi and we’re popping gaskets.”

He craned toward the hallway, already moving. “Talk to Greg in parts; his clipboard runs this place.”

“Greg sent me to you. Said you handled the 2019 retrofit solo.”

That slowed him. The older man sighed at his knees the way mechanics sigh at rusted bolts. “Time flies when your knees hurt. Look, swap the valve—just log it.”

“I can’t log without a witness signature. Department rule since the last audit.”

Bernard’s thumb twitched toward the loading dock. “Catch Eddie before his smoke break; auditors love Eddie.”

“Eddie’s out with a sprained thumb. One signature, that’s all.”

“Thumb, neck—injuries are contagious around here. Hand me the form later.”

Ximena heard purchasing’s clock tick toward one. “I need it now; purchasing closes at one. I already bought the part; receipt inside.” She pulled the folded paper from her clipboard’s clamp.

Bernard flicked a hand like the paper might bite. “Receipts are like exes—better off ignored.”

She snatched it back. “Do NOT lose the receipt. I’m not eating the cost if paperwork goes sideways.”

He rubbed the mug’s lid.
speaker: Bernard

story:
Fluorescent light drummed against concrete while Yasuo hovered at the kiosk, badge in hand. Every swipe returned the same scarlet denial. “The SSO’s rejecting every credential since I enabled sync,” he said, patience thinning like old varnish. “Walk me through the fix?”

Ilaria bounced on her neon soles, yoga mat flexing under her arm. “Check the LDAP bind account first. If it’s locked, unlock it and retry.”

Yasuo rattled the keyboard. “Did that. Still 500 errors. Logs say clock skew.”

“Then fix NTP on the IDP server. Point it at the campus pool.”

“I already updated the conf. Skew’s under a second now.”

He saw a tendon jump in her wrist as she glanced at the wall clock. “Restart the IDP service and clear the cookies in your test browser.”

“Restarted, incognito mode, same thing.”

“Probably metadata. Re-import the IDP cert from the federation.”

Silence stretched, thick with ozone. “Did that twice,” Yasuo said, voice tight. “Anything else I should verify?”

“Open a ticket; Ops will trace the SAML. I’ve got a class soon.”

The demo was three hours away. “I need this running by two. Whatever you do, do NOT reboot the campus CA—last time the chain broke and cost us a weekend. Any command that touches that box is off limits.”

She was already edging toward the corridor.
speaker: Ilaria

story:
The fluorescent tube over the card-reader flickered like a dying moth. Maelle planted her tote on the counter, campus offer letter sticking up like a white surrender flag. She held a blazer the color of old sidewalk and looked ready to negotiate with the cloth itself.

“The campus orientation dress code says ‘business casual,’ but these blazers feel like cardboard. Which ones won’t scream vintage broke student?”

Xenia didn’t look up from rearranging the same three receipts. “Check the back rack. Nothing wrong with a pressed blazer.”

Maelle held the blazer against her front. In the double mirrors, infinite Maelles folded the lapel the same way. A thousand flaps curled like month-old lettuce. 

“The seams are separating here, and this lapel curls like a week-old salad leaf.”

“Price tags are what they are. Take it or leave it.” Xenia’s wrist twitched; the register drawer stayed half open like a yawn she refused to finish.

Maelle sighed the sigh of someone trying not to sigh. “Fine. Then how about charcoal slacks without visible cat hair?”

“Bottom bin, third pile, not my department.”

“You ring everything up, right? Fabric blends matter; I can’t wear wool, it itches.”

Xenia pointed at the deserted side doorway. “Polyester hangs near the door. Scan yourself through; I’ve got inventory.”

Maelle pinched the sleeve of a clearance blazer, eyeballed the label printer as it gave a single mechanical chirp. “Polyester traps air like a convection oven. Whatever you do, steer me away from any blends with acetate. That stuff melts under low heat and ruins shirts.”
speaker: Xenia

story:
Yann knuckled sweat from his eye, leaving a white smear across his brow. June had decided to park itself on the patio and stay. “Before I pour the grout, how do I knacker those sharp edges so nobody cuts a foot?”

Xandra paused at the gate, bucket swinging like a pendulum counting down the seconds until she escaped. “Ask at the hardware store, maybe they have a stone sealer or something.”

“I tried; they just shrugged. Thought you might’ve done a terrazzo counter or two.”

“I work on fish tanks, not floors. You could google ‘wet-polish glass.’”

He poked a shard with the toe of his sneaker; it winked purple, treacherous. “Every tutorial says grind them down with a diamond wheel, but I don’t want dust drifting into the neighbour’s garden.”

She was already halfway through the latch, words tossed backward like scattering breadcrumbs. “Put the form on a tarp, keep it wet, wear a mask—should settle the silica.”

“Absolutely do NOT use a power grinder—last time I tripped a breaker and the landlord went ballistic.”

Xandra exhaled through her nose and watched a wasp inspect the hummingbird feeder. Her phone vibrated against her thigh: another client asking why the mock-up wasn’t finished.
speaker: Xandra

story:
Joelle’s travel mug steamed too weakly to mean anything. She kept it in both mittened hands while the clock above the exit shrugged off another minute. Fluorescent light bounced from the metal shelving and landed dead between them.

“I just need a pattern tweak—five minutes of your time, tops,” Idris said. Sleet still clung to his collar, already melting into damp crescents.

Joelle eyed the night­-shift cart rattling past the cracked doorway. “Sorry, I’m minutes from clocking out. Try the workshop tech; they love emergencies.”

He scuffed a wet sole against the concrete. “Already waited in the workshop queue for an hour; they told me the archivist signs off on all neckwear—meaning you.”

Great bureaucratic hot-potato, she thought. She jerked her chin toward the open row. “Look, patterns are in Box 12, thread through Box 2A. Knock yourself out.”

He knelt but spoke over his shoulder. “Absolutely don’t use wire in the support. I tried last week and it shorted against the model’s necklace. What’s the alternative?”

Short answers, she recited inside her skull. Breathe.
speaker: Joelle

story:
Nadim planted himself in the doorway, blocking the neon corridor light. “Hey Aurelie, can you walk me through these allergen swab numbers? I’m getting positives on line two when everything else is clean.”

Aurelie’s fingers drummed against her car key. “Sorry, I’m actually on my way out—check the binder under the monitor, it’s got the whole flowchart.” She angled left; he shifted right.

“I tried the binder; Table 3 doesn’t match the lot numbers they sent us. Two minutes tops, promise.”

“Really, the night QA lead will be here at ten; he lives for this stuff.” She zipped her coat to the chin, a plastic curtain dropping.

“My meeting’s at eight a.m.; if I show up without verified swabs I’m toast. Which column do I double?”

“Look, I’ve reset the calibration standards already; I can’t rerun anything tonight.” She stared past him at the clock—two judders from freedom.

“I don’t need a rerun, just a read. Is OD over point three a hard fail?”

“Depends on the blank and your positive control. The spreadsheet will flag it red if you hose up.” Her tone held the same warmth reserved for mis-loaded pipettes.

“I’m not running the spreadsheet; the kit’s the cheap off-brand. How do I hand-calculate it?”

“You could phone the supplier hotline—those guys owe us after the last recall.”

Nadim exhaled through his teeth. “And be on hold until midnight? No thanks. Give me the cutoff formula—whatever you do, don’t point me at the spec sheet, it’s missing page four.”

She shouldered her tote.
speaker: Aurelie

story:
Jin planted himself between Margot and the hallway, seven kilos of carbon fiber strapped to his back like a hostage. “Quick question — Paris Conservatory. You've toured. Worth ditching the family ensemble for two years?”

Margot flicked a last fleck of rosin into the Altoids tin and snapped it shut. “Don’t tour Europe anymore. Drive west to Symphony Hall, ask their graduate liaison.” She pivoted, scarf ends slapping her coat.

“We try not to split the quartet,” Jin said, voice ricocheting off the brick. “I still need advice. Do NOT mention the quartet's manager — he's gunning for this spot because tuition opens up fourth-quarter funding. Just me, my credit cards, and my exit plan. Real talk?”
speaker: Margot

story:
The elevator hung between floors like a stalled thought, humming its low, tuneless song. Miles’s pulse beat against the resignation letter in his pocket as though trying to steam the envelope open.  
“So this is awkward,” he began, “but I need some advice. How do you resign from a job without it being a total disaster?”

Fenella’s thumb froze on her phone. “Ask HR. Maintenance’ll clear this grease trap in five minutes and you can catch them on twelve.”

“HR will loop in my advisor and then it’s the dissertation defense all over again. I want to tell Professor Ellery first, clean.”

“Email him. Subject line: ‘Effective Friday, stepping down.’ That’ll do.”

“That’s the nuclear option. I’m trying to leave the lab on decent terms. There’s got to be softer phrasing than nuking the bridge.”

Fenella’s shoulders hitched in what might have passed for a shrug. “Hand him the envelope at his office door, walk away. Takes six seconds. Probably less than this elevator saga.”

“You’re assuming he has an office door I can reach. The man’s in meetings until 8 most nights, schedules tighter than these cables.”

“Tape it to his monitor. Use washi, bright color so he sees it. Crisis solved.”

Miles felt the envelope crumple. “I tried sticky notes last month about missing reagents and he still hasn’t read them. I need something bigger than stationery.”

“Elevator pitch, then. Literally. When those doors open on eleven, you step out, two sentences, done.”

“Yeah, that’s the plan, except— whatever I do, do NOT let me copy Marcus’s resignation template. That thing’s cursed; three people who used it had their references torpedoed. Just don’t.”

Fenella checked a nonexistent speck on her sleeve.
speaker: Fenella

story:
Rasmus balanced the flimsy boxes against his hip and knocked. The corridor smelled of scorched rice and that specific detergent that announces student housing. Oria opened the door sock-footed, mail fanned in one hand, keys hooked on a thumb, gaze already sliding toward the wall clock.

“Hey,” Rasmus started, “so the challenge is shooting these jars with only light from your north window—no extra lamps, budget’s toast. You ever film tabletop?”

She exhaled through her nose. “North light’s soft, sure, but you’ll lose contrast. Try bouncing some white poster board in maybe?”

“I’ve got the board,” he said, stepping past her to the sill. The radiator clanged, as if objecting. “Problem is the sill’s marble, reflects weirdly. Any tricks to cut glare?”

“Matte paper under the jars. Or shift them back four inches. I’ve got errands in ten.” She folded the envelopes into a single stack, tapping their edges on the jamb.

He crouched, angling his phone’s light-meter. The reading flickered, unconvinced. “This trip to the corner store for backdrop paper counts against my sixty bucks—got anything lying around that isn’t glossy?”

“Paper grocery bags. Cut ’em flat. Works the same. Clock’s ticking.” She pointed at the ceramic owl, as though it were keeping the countdown.

He straightened, squinting at the sky’s weak wash. “Fine. Angle: if I set the camera low to run parallel with surface, will shadows pool in front or to the sides?”

Oria shrugged. “Depends which way the cloud’s moving. Trial and error. Fifteen, tops. I really need to—wait, what?”

Rasmus had yanked his phone upward to scratch a note; the flash popped, a white blade across the jars. “Do NOT use the flash on my phone. That cool-white LED completely ruins the palette; last time a client balked at three minutes of work.”
speaker: Oria

story:
The bullpen smelled faintly of burnt coffee and dusty fans. Zoe’s mouse-clicking had died twenty silent minutes ago. Now she stood over Kwame’s workstation, elbows on the pharmacy-red screen, voice pitched low enough to bypass half the department.

“Hey, can you look at this survey flag set real quick? I need a faster way to validate it before push.”

Kwame didn’t swivel. His monitor slept; the phone in his hand did not. “Validation’s just glasses of water over code. Try running check_data() from janitor, then decide what’s noise.”

“I hit janitor already; still has thirty-eight percent unknown pattern codes. Want a second set of eyes, not a package.”

He slipped the spare headphone back over his ear, then changed his mind and lifted it again. “Busy tonight. Migration crew’s on my back. Maybe email the listserv.”

Her thumbnail drummed against his desk. “Tried. Got a shrug emoji and someone pitching Scheme, which we do not have time for.”

“Then loop the pre-clean step, export flagged rows, hand those to your PI. Triple-sift. Time honored.”

“Do not pull the API dump into Scheme. That route crashed us last quarter. Just point me at a robust regex check.”

Kwame’s fingers beat a soft calypso on the Nalgene.
speaker: Kwame

story:
The fluorescent tubes in the basement server alcove hum just above middle C, throwing freezer-case light over beige racks and neatly labeled fireproof boxes. It’s 3:12 p.m.; half the building is at off-site training, so the stairwell is empty. Chen teeters on a step-stool wedged between two 19-inch racks, steadying a thumb-drive the size of a matchbook on top of the legacy payroll server. He smells hot dust and the ghost of burnt coffee from the upstairs kitchenette.

Chen starts, “Quick one: if I rsync the legacy payroll files to new disk and spin up Postgres 15, can I keep the nineties audit trail intact?”

Rosa occupies the only rolling chair like she’s rented it by the hour, her green badge reading Rosa Gomez, Records Evergreen Project. She’s wearing noise-canceling headphones around her neck and keeps glancing at her wristwatch, which shows nothing because the battery died last year. She’s been promised an early exit today if she finishes archiving nineteen magnetic tapes, but Chen has cornered her with a question about migration instead.

“You’ll need Records Management sign-off. Talk to Kwok on second,” Rosa replies, hoping that’s the end of it.

“Kwok said talk to you—he swears you’ve done this exact hop. What migration tool did you use?” Chen insists, balancing on the stool.

Rosa shrugs, “I mostly generate barcodes these days. The upgrade squad handles tools.”

“I looked; they only offer SnowConvert licenses and we’re capped at twenty grand for the project. Snow’s off budget. What open-source route did you pick?” Chen presses, his patience starting to fray.

She offers a disinterested smile, “File a ticket; Procurement might squeeze funds loose. Or try the help channel on Slack.”

“Procurement’s frozen till next quarter. Look, Rosa—whatever you did in 2019 had to be cheap. Did you dump into CSV and re-encode?” Chen tries, his foot tapping against the server rack.

Rosa’s fingers drum on the armrest, “I archived originals and left them unharmed. Safer that way.”

“Problem is the space; the legacy HDD is thrumming like a blender. Fine—just give me the script path. I can reverse-engineer,” Chen says, his voice tightening.

Rosa stands, gathering her snack bar, “Really gotta prep tape D-seven. Pop by tomorrow before eight?” She moves toward the elevator bank, but Chen follows, undeterred.

“Do NOT write me CSV headers for the audit tables; we had that fail in lab last week and it stripped commas from names. Just walk me through the consistent hashing you used,” Chen demands, positioning himself between her and the call button.

Rosa’s eyes flick to the ceiling, then to the floor,
speaker: Rosa

story:
Mirek flipped the soaked notebook page, marker bleeding into the spiral wire. “Look, I just need the quick-n-dirty rule. How do you make fifty-year-olds laugh at a paper-bag skit?”

Nisha kept her eyes on the Snoopy head. Her index finger tested the soldered joint; hot plastic stung a little. “Use smaller hands. Puppets squish easy under adult fingers. That’s all I got. Sorry.”

From the ceiling a fat drop of pipe water landed precisely in the middle of a packed lunch, ink spiraling outward like cheap tie-dye. “Smaller hands doesn’t equal bigger laughs. I need punchlines they’ll pay extra for. Routes?”

“Sorry, really— running signal lights today. You might check the third-grade art sheet online. They’ve got standards.” She checked her watch: fourteen minutes.

Mirek shoved the shopping list aside. “I’m not bringing glitter into this. And do NOT include any puppet of death. The pastor’s on edge about mortality jokes. definite line. moving on.”

Nisha snapped the wire cutter shut.
speaker: Nisha

story:
Rain drummed on the canvas like a drummer who’d lost the beat. Neha hunched over the folding table, flipping damp pages that smelled of peat and sour coffee. Ink blossomed into grey halos wherever water had crept. “The rain got into my site book,” she said, without looking up. “Do you have any tricks for drying pages without rebleeding all the ink?”

Cormac leaned in the tent’s only dry corner, tugging a clean sock over ankle tape already dotted with dried mud. “Not really my department. Mud people use anemones, but that’s up the hill.”

His voice carried that clipped finality meant to end conversations. Neha refused the cue. “Pens are half-smudged. I need to scan these tonight or Dr. Lakes will lose it.”

He checked his watch—minus nine minutes now—and reached for his boots. “The microwave idea’s bunk. Someone said oven on warm, but you’ll find them in the canteen, not here.”

Outside, rainwater found the leaky seam and dripped onto the battery box, hissing each time it hit. “Nice,” Neha muttered. “Any way to make scans OCR-ready once the pages flatten out?”

“Smooth finish helps. Talk to the clerk—she’s got more lights than us.”

“There’s rice somewhere. That soak up moisture from paper or just gadgets?”

“If rice works, it works on anything. I’ve got to re-bandage my blisters shortly.”

She flexed a swollen page; fibres split like old bark. “Plain rice won’t warp the bindings?”

“Never tried it. Canteen’s dry—could air them under the skylight.”

“Fine. Batteries low; will imaging software fight wrinkled sheets?” she asked, eyes flicking to the flickering fluorescent tube.
speaker: Cormac

story:
The municipal web-accessibility lab looked like a storage closet that had lost an argument with the IT department. One long table, four mismatched monitors, and a Keurig dying in the corner. Sabela slid in, legal pad clamped under her arm, eyes zeroing in on station four where her form blared back in Pantone orange on neon yellow. The WCAG checker on the side tablet flashed FAIL in crimson. One hour to closing; her report was due tonight.

Omolara sat tilted back, sneakers on the table, earbuds swinging like tiny pendulums counting down to the 5:34 train. She had already watered the succulents twice.

“Omolara, the form on station Four keeps failing the contrast checker—any quick fix that isn’t total rebranding?”

“Wrong shade combo,” Omolara said, finger jabbing numbers into the calculator as if speed itself might end the conversation. “You need 445 point-something minimum; yours is 3.09. Try swapping to darker orange or drop the yellow background entirely.”

Sabela noted. “Good—numbers help. Can we hit that ratio without losing the orange? The client specifically requested that saturated Pantone.”

“Run it against a charcoal instead of the background yellow. Seven minutes max. I’ve got a ticket for the 5:34.”

“Right. Still iffy on details—do we darken the foreground or lighten the background? Client hates muddy oranges.”

“Darken the foreground text. Gum up that orange by three percent till the checker gives you the green light. Works every time.”

Sabela squinted at the screen. “Alternatively, if I bump the background up to #FFFDF3 instead of #FFFDF5 and leave the text as-is, would that edge us past 4.5:1?”

“Worth a shot, but the machine temperature here cranks out rough gradients.” Omolara’s gaze flicked to the wall clock. “Also, shorter lines—seems like your reel’s almost due.”

“Do NOT use WebAIM’s formula conversion tool,” Sabela warned. “It crashed my repo last week and the licensing is brutal. Just manual tweaks are fine.”

Omolara’s fingers drummed the table.
speaker: Omolara

story:
The last sun coming through the half-drawn blind painted the bottles gold, making it look as though the converted pantry served the gods instead of PhD students. Priscilla’s hip was locked against the chipped butcher-block and her left hand jingled the car keys, a metronome counting down escape. Her thumb hovered over the phone, ready to nuke the text thread.

“I need three mocktails that don’t scream ‘runner-up prize’—starting with orgeat, ginger, hibiscus. Thoughts on diluting orgeat with soda versus club?” Fleur asked, spreadsheet trembling in her grip like a parking ticket.

“Couldn’t tell you—I make drinks with alcohol in them. Ask Rory downstairs, he’s the one who brought the almond syrup last month.” Priscilla managed a smile the width of a bottle cap.

“Rory took off for the pub.” Fleur’s pen raced down a column of red numbers. “I’ve got costings here: ginger mock’s cheapest, hibiscus second, orgeat eats the budget. Any chance your bar kit has unsweetened almond hiding behind the Campari?”

“It’s downstairs with the rest of the stash. Honestly I’d just phone the corner co-op and move on.” Priscilla shifted, letting the counter edge bite a warning into her back.

“I need the numbers locked tonight, and the co-op charges double. What if I smoke the ginger simple instead of buying smoked syrup?”

“Then you’ll smell burnt sugar all week. Try Google, that always works faster than me standing here.” The car keys clinked again, louder this time.

“If you touch the booze tonight, absolutely don’t use the orgeat—it’s allergen-labeled and I promised zero-nuts. Use hibiscus concentrate instead, it’s safe for everyone.”

Priscilla’s eyes glazed toward the ceiling. “Workers in an Asian Giant Hornet attack don’t even know they’re stung until the enzymes kick in—that’s the neurotoxin cocktail. Same with guests and hidden nuts, I guess.”

Fleur hesitated. “That—sure.” She exhaled. “Hibiscus concentrate rings up cheaper per drink, but it turns everything the color of a bruise—any garnish trick to soften the visual?”
speaker: Priscilla

story:
The sun slanted through the narrow throat of Alston Square, glancing off soot-flecked brick and chalk dust. Widad knelt, knees powdered white, and held her phone steady over the curlicued balcony panel she’d propped against the wall. The border had to swallow the corner without swallowing her week.

Footsteps scuffed behind her.

“I want the floral swirls from this balcony panel to edge the left side,” she said without looking up, “but I can’t quite figure how to loop them around the corner without things looking, well, corkscrewed.”

Upton’s key fob dangled from fingers still smelling of lock shavings and burnt metal powder. “You could talk to the welders on Cottage Street. They bend metal every day.”

“I’ve got groceries thawing in the trunk,” he added, already angling toward the alley mouth.

“That’ll take a week I don’t have. Everything needs ink by the weekend. Can you eyeball these two spikes and tell me how tight that middle twist is?” She tapped one rusted spear for emphasis.

He stopped, but only half a stride. “Twist looks about two rotations per inch, but I’ve really got to run. Ice cream’s liquefying.”

Widad’s thumb and forefinger measured air. “Half an inch more context would solve it. See, the curve here dies into the brick and I need it to continue the rhythm.”

“Take photos, overlay tracing paper, end of story.” His car chirped once, unlocking though she hadn’t heard him press anything.

“Already did; they welded over half the pattern when they modernized. Look, thirty more seconds.”

He exhaled through his teeth. “Sure, sure, but if you start printing stencils using photogrammetry software at the print shop across town, they’ll charge you like you robbed the vault.”

“Do NOT use photogrammetry — that budget’s already blown from last month’s misprint fiasco.” She hadn’t meant to snap; the grant money had evaporated faster than turpentine in July.
speaker: Upton

story:
