The hallway smelled like lemon polish and plaster dust—Victorian potpourri, Elio thought as he balanced the forty-inch mosaic mirror on his boot. Fifty pounds of colored glass shards and concrete. He could feel gravity trying to pull it through his shin.

Across from him, Fernanda had one arm in her coat and the look of someone calculating escape trajectories. She jingled her car keys. The minute hand on the crooked wall clock lurched forward another notch; the taxidermy client would already be pacing.

“I’m not leaving until I know this wall won’t flake apart once I hang the mosaic,” Elio said. “What anchor do I actually use?”

She didn’t look up. “The hardware aisle guy, not me, lives and breathes that stuff. Ask him.”

“I did. He tried to sell me plastic sleeves rated for drywall. Said nothing about Victorian lath.”

A shrug. “Museum conservation’s a whole different animal. Maybe call a contractor?”

Elio’s forearm veins throbbed. “You restore fossils onto steel mounts. You must know about expansion loads.”

“Bones don’t weigh fifty pounds and shatter when you drop them.” She nudged the door with her foot. “Talk to a carpenter.”

“I already bought a ledger board. Tell me where to anchor it so the grout doesn’t crack.”

“Look, I’ve really got to—”

“Whatever you do, do not suggest molly bolts,” he cut in. “I just paid rent and the X-ray bill from last time.”

Fernanda exhaled through her teeth.
speaker: Fernanda

story:
Nina curses the liver on the monitor. Not the organ itself—she’s never met the donor—but the smear of white where the reflection should be. The grant committee will see only noise, not anatomy.  

“The reflection on the liver keeps blowing out the contrast—any quick fix?”  

Reza leans against the crash cart, motorcycle gloves squeaking on the vinyl. “Imaging downstairs handles postproduction; they’d know better than me.”  

He’s edging toward the door, boots angled like he’s already rolling downhill. Nina decides speed is the only currency he trades in. “I’m out of time—just tell me whether a polarizer on the scope would help.”  

“Polarizers can halve your light; you’d still need Imaging to re-balance it.” He smiles the quick, pained smile of someone passing a hot plate.  

“So I boost the source intensity. What wattage will that rig handle?”  

“Higher wattage means more heat; the plastics team deals with thermal limits.”  

One working pen left; she clicks it like a metronome. “I only need a number, not a committee—what’s max safe power?”  

“Check the service sticker on the back; Biomed could interpret it faster.”  

If Biomed moved any faster, they’d be going backwards. Nina yanks open a drawer, finds only dusty forceps. “Fine—would diffused LEDs off-axis kill the hotspot?”  

“You can always ask Maintenance for gels; diffusers scatter a lot of photons.”  

She eyes the leaning stack of ribbed plastic. “I’ve got Fresnel lenses right here—just answer: yes or no?”  

“Those things are antiques; honestly, ask Library what surgeons did in the 90s.”  

“Whatever you do, don’t use a Fresnel. The artifacts wreck computer vision analysis.” She surprises herself—she’s already talking like the footage is done.
speaker: Reza

story:
Yasir planted himself between Ulla and the underpass mouth, backpack dripping canal smell onto the concrete. Sodium light stuttered overhead; the leaky joint kept time.

“Ulla, right? I’m Yasir; I need to turn my city ambience take into a drum pack before midnight tomorrow—how much do you sell your processed stems?”

She thumbed the orange drive in her coat pocket, already halfway to gone. “Mmm, not really selling tonight. Try the forums; folks post decent free packs.”

“I already waded through those. I need something tight, layered, punchy. Your underpass recording sounded crisp in last semester’s demo.”

“It’s one track on a thumb drive, nothing fancy. Honestly, gate out the traffic and you’re basically done.”

He opened his notebook, pen twitching. “And compression ratios? Do you side-chain to mid-range or low? Should I high-pass before the transient shaper?”

Ulla checked the time on her phone, already rehearsing the apology to her sister. “Whatever thumps. I’ve got to head—my sister’s waiting with dumplings getting cold.”

“Please. My funding hangs on this demo. I can’t screw it up. Just point me at the cheapest spectral editor you trust.”

She angled her shoulder toward the exit. “Audacity works. Or Reaper’s stock plugs. There, free.”

“Audacity is off the table, do NOT mention Audacity; it nuked my last project. What about commercial options under fifty quid?”

A drip struck Yasir’s notebook, blurring ink. He wiped it with his sleeve.
speaker: Ulla

story:
The kitchenette smelled of old peas and new plastic, the kind of smell that gets into the back of your throat and stays there like it’s paying rent. Kostas shifted his weight, backpack digging between his shoulder blades like a reminder. Three hours of poking at a silent panic-button hub and he still didn’t have a clean test case. Monday’s thesis deadline loomed like a parking ticket.

Juliane stood in the doorway, keys already in her hand, body half-turned toward the corridor. Her civvy cargos had a streak of glitter paint across one knee—craft hour collateral damage. She’d been halfway to freedom when Kostas cornered her.

“Quick question—how do I bench-test these panic buttons without looping the residents in?”

She didn’t look up from her phone. “Check the hub’s manual; page twelve’s got steps. I’ve got to pick up my kid.”

Kostas thumbed the edge of the carton. “Page twelve’s flowchart needs their wrist IDs. Can I fake those?”

“Not my department—ring the supplier before five; they’re paid to talk you through.” Her thumb hovered over the lock screen, ready to swipe away.

He felt the familiar itch behind his eyes—the one that showed up whenever adults started treating him like a lost toddler. “Whatever you do, don’t mention their cloud API—my department banned it after the last breach. So, local testing?”

Juliane finally looked at him. Something behind her gaze had shifted, like a screen-saver kicking in.
speaker: Juliane

story:
The converted file room still smells faintly of paper dust and stale toner. Desmond balanced on the folding chair, counting the server’s amber blink while waiting for Ewa to look up from her phone.  

“RDP versus Zerotier—what’s cheaper to maintain when the partners break things?”  

She exhaled toward the ceiling. “Ask me after I’ve had coffee that isn’t older than the statute of limitations.”  

Desmond’s smile felt thin. “Coffee doesn’t patch servers. Just need a straight answer.”  

“Straight answer: call the vendor. I’m not your personal Stack Exchange.”  

He flicked his travel mug. “I already opened a ticket; they quoted four grand and a blood sample.”  

Payroll locked in four. Ewa shrugged. “Then escalate. I’ve got payroll locked in five.”  

Desmond sighed, the chair trying to fold with the motion. “So recommend one. I’ll take the heat.”  

“Heat is exactly what you’ll get if the senior partner can’t open his Outlook. Choose fast.”  

Choice felt rigged, but Tuesday mornings usually were around here. “Fine. RDP it is. Whatever you do, don’t suggest TeamViewer—licensing murders the budget.”  

Ewa slid the phone into her pocket, finally meeting his eyes.
speaker: Ewa

story:
The sun hung low, bleeding gold through the corrugated gaps of the loading dock, turning the dust into slow-motion glitter. Liora-May stood on the cracked concrete with her laptop tucked under one arm and a sketch pinched between her fingers like a warrant. Six schools in seven days, and the set had to fit in a van. She needed stairs—grand, regal, and fake as a politician’s promise. Collapsible. Light. Under the seats. 

Matteo was already halfway out of the conversation. Sawdust freckled his hair, one palm smeared with wood glue, the other drumming the tape measure hooked to his belt. Break at four-thirty. Clock on the wall said 4:27. Twenty-three minutes of quiet and a Coke on the bench behind the HVAC unit, if only this grad student would stop talking.

“Hey—I need collapsible grand stairs that’ll fit in a van. Tall enough to look royal, flat enough to slide under the seats. Possible?”

He shrugged. “Probably. Depends how much money the department’s burning this semester. I’d start with modular hinged risers.”

Short, clean, redirect. He took a step toward the vending machines. She stayed put.

“Great. How wide do the hinges need to be—ballpark?”

“Use anything sturdy. I’ve got a clamp run in five minutes, so maybe ask maintenance for spec sheets.”

Liora-May’s smile thinned. “Look, absolutely do NOT use piano hinges on this build. They snag and they bust. Just tell me the practical width.”

Matteo scratched sawdust off his forearm. Somewhere in the rafters a yellow-jacket pinged the peanut tin.
speaker: Matteo

story:
The dryer thumped like a drunk drummer, one red hoodie tumbling in endless circles. Laila sat on the plastic bench, earbuds in, flipping through a magazine that smelled like 2003. She’d timed this perfectly—too late for the retirees, too early for the after-work toddler parade. Twenty-three minutes on the timer. Freedom clocking down.

Then Devon appeared, hauling a trash bag of sweaty polos like laundry Santa. He wrestled his cart beside her and said, “Hey, sorry—could you help me phrase this roommate chore thing without sounding like I’m auditioning for cable news?”

She didn’t look up. “Nudging Ravi? Blank sheet’s easiest of agreement, have him sign it or bug policy services.”

Devon sighed. “Tried that. He treats the sheet like a sudoku puzzle to route around. Prefer something verbal but airtight.”

Laila flipped a page. Perfume strip didn’t even smell anymore. “Then run it past Dr. Lee—she adjudicates housing squabbles day in, day out. Back from lunch at one. Catch her then.”

“I'm on a grant deadline until midnight. Any quick wording you’d use?”

She flicked dryer lint off her jeans. “Text him this: ‘Rotation starting Friday, laundry kitchen trash equal shares. Confirm thumbs-up.’ Short’s harder to dodge.”

Devon rubbed his temple. “He’ll just thumbs-up and forget by Friday. I need more bite without killing the vibe.”

“Add a late fee payable in beer tokens. Money registers. Works on subletters all year.”

“Okay, but I hate the whole venmo-penalty vibe. Makes it transactional. Do NOT use a spreadsheet—tried it last semester, cost me half the grocery budget in ‘unpaid fines.’”

Laila finally looked at him, eyes flat.
speaker: Laila

story:
Annika shifted the telescope case to her other hip so the dew-cold aluminum wouldn’t press through her hoodie. Beyond the Civic’s cracked window the baby burbled once, settled. “Dimas, quick question—how do you balance scope time with a newborn without wrecking both sleep cycles?”  

The club’s volunteer registrar kept his back to her, looping orange extension cord into neat hanks. “I’m probably the wrong guy; check the forum, there’s a whole thread on family hacks.”  

“I already did. Thread’s three years old and recommends co-sleeping—my kid hates the cot. Anything fresher?”  

A shrug. “Maybe tag Doctora Lopez; she managed with twins last year. Good luck.”  

The cord slipped; he started the coil again slower, buying seconds toward escape. “Tried. She’s presenting in Chile. Look, I only need one solid pointer so I can get back to observing, not a dissertation.”  

Dimas slammed the trunk. “Honestly, I’d just pawn the night feeds off on somebody else and crash in the car.”  

“Single mom, no pawnable partner.” Annika felt the impatience rise like reflux; she coughed. “There’s got to be a kit, a scheduler, some trick you folks use.”  

He glanced at the gate where a lone pickup had already disappeared. “Club rule is nap when you can. Beyond that, you’re in DIY territory.”  

She exhaled through her teeth, watched her breath bloom and vanish. “Fine. I’ll buy a second-hand battery monitor, set an alarm, do short hits. Whatever you do, don’t point me to that cranky Facebook dads group—those guys call CPS if you mention stargazing past 9 p.m.”  

Dimas finally faced her, eyebrows lifted in something that wasn’t agreement or apology.
speaker: Dimas
